common_name: Aureomaculata Ventricosa Hosta (Gold-Centered Blue Plantain Lily)

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, evenly moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade, giving a little morning sun where summers are cool to intensify the spring gold coloring.

directions: Aureomaculata is a sport of Hosta ventricosa named for its blotched gold leaf centers, which emerge in a striking mix of chartreuse and gold streaked over green in spring before fading to nearly solid green as summer heat sets in, the reverse pattern from its better-known sibling Aureomarginata. The broad, glossy, quilted leaves carry the same deep-violet, funnel-shaped flowers as the species on tall scapes in mid- to late summer. Like the straight species it tolerates more shade and summer heat than many hostas, though the transient spring variegation is best appreciated up close in a border or container rather than relied on as a season-long feature. Divide congested clumps only occasionally in spring, since it is a steady but unhurried grower.

common_name: Bloom-A-Thon Red Azalea (Reblooming Compact Scarlet Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun; Bloom-A-Thon Red reblooms from April through the first hard fall frost rather than in a single spring flush.

directions: Bloom-A-Thon Red is the scarlet-flowered member of the Proven Winners ColorChoice reblooming azalea series (patented as Rhododendron x 'RLH1-1P2', USPP 21,562), bred as a sun-tolerant alternative to the Encore line with an extended bloom window that runs from a heavy April flush through repeat color into early summer and again until frost. It grows noticeably larger than its Hot Pink, Lavender, and White series siblings, forming a broad, upright-rounded shrub that works well as a specimen or informal hedge rather than a low foundation plant. Give it moist, acidic, well-drained soil and more direct morning sun than older azalea types tolerate to sustain the long rebloom cycle, and trim lightly right after the spring flush so developing summer and fall buds are not removed.

common_name: You and Me Romance Hydrangea (Double-Flowered Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Romance carries the same reblooming, double-flowered habit as its You and Me series sibling Together, so light pruning preserves the earliest flush.

directions: Romance is a companion release to Together in the You and Me series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, distinguished by loosely rounded flower heads made up of double to triple-petaled florets rather than a single tight dome. Individual sepals open in soft, fresh pink shades on neutral-to-alkaline soil and shift toward pale blue-mauve in acidic soil, giving each flower head a layered, ruffled texture as the florets slowly fill in over a long summer bloom period. Because flowering continues from both overwintered and current-season stems, plants still produce a strong late-season show even where a hard winter or aggressive pruning removes the previous year's growth. Grow in evenly moist, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and limit pruning to spent blooms and dead wood so the earliest old-wood flowers are not sacrificed.

common_name: You and Me Forever Hydrangea (Compact Double-Flowered Reblooming Mophead)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Forever stays more compact than its You and Me series sibling Together, fitting smaller borders and large containers.

directions: Forever is a compact member of the You and Me series of reblooming bigleaf hydrangeas, bred to stay noticeably smaller and denser than its series sibling Together while carrying the same fully double, star-shaped florets packed into a rounded flower head. Blooms open a deep, saturated pink on neutral-to-alkaline soil and shift to true blue with soil acidification, held on unusually sturdy, well-branched stems that keep the heavy double flower heads from flopping even after summer rain. Because it sets buds on both old and new wood, a plant that dies back over a cold winter or is pruned hard still produces a full late-summer flush rather than skipping a season. Give it evenly moist, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and prune only lightly right after the first bloom flush to protect the following old-wood buds.
